title: Atoms, Molecules and Ions
description: What atoms are made of, how the periodic table is organized, how ions and compounds are named, and what a mole is.
overview: All matter is built from a little over a hundred kinds of atoms. What makes one element different from another is the number of protons in its nucleus. How atoms combine into molecules and ions, and how many of them are in a sample you can weigh, is the foundation for every quantitative idea in chemistry.

This chapter describes the experiments that revealed the structure of the atom, introduces isotopes and atomic mass, tours the periodic table, then covers chemical formulas, nomenclature and the mole.
objectives: Describe the evidence for electrons, the nucleus and neutrons.
Use atomic number, mass number and isotope notation, and compute an average atomic mass.
Locate groups, periods, metals, nonmetals and metalloids on the periodic table.
Predict ion charges, write formulas of ionic compounds, and name ionic and molecular compounds.
Convert among mass, moles and number of particles using molar mass and Avogadro’s constant.

sections.title: The structure of the atom
body: In 1808 John Dalton proposed that each element consists of identical, indivisible atoms; that atoms of different elements differ in mass; and that compounds form when atoms combine in small whole-number ratios. Dalton’s theory explained the laws of conservation of mass and definite proportions. Its one great error was that atoms are indivisible.

In 1897 J. J. Thomson showed that cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles, because electric and magnetic fields deflect them. From the size of the deflections he found their charge-to-mass ratio, e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹. In 1909 Robert Millikan measured the charge on tiny oil droplets and found they carry whole multiples of 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the charge of one electron. Combined with e/m, this gives the electron’s mass: 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg, about 1/1836 of a hydrogen atom. Thomson pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it, the plum-pudding model.

In 1909 Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired α particles (He²⁺ nuclei) at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but about one in 8000 was deflected through a large angle, some bouncing back. Rutherford wrote that it was “as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back.” The result is impossible if positive charge is spread through the atom. Instead, nearly all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a tiny **nucleus**, about 10⁻¹⁵ m across, in an atom about 10⁻¹⁰ m across. If the nucleus were a marble, the atom would be about a kilometer wide. The electrons occupy the space around it.
In 1932 James Chadwick identified the **neutron**, an uncharged particle with nearly the same mass as the proton, which accounts for the nuclear mass not explained by protons alone.

sections.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
body: The **atomic number** Z is the number of protons in the nucleus. It defines the element: every atom with Z = 6 is carbon. In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals Z. The **mass number** A is the number of protons plus neutrons, so the number of neutrons is N = A − Z.

A nuclide is written ᴬ_{Z}X, for example ¹²₆C. **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, such as carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14. They have nearly identical chemistry, because chemistry is governed by electrons, but different masses and, for some, an unstable nucleus (see the chapter on nuclear chemistry).

Atomic masses are measured in **atomic mass units**. One u is defined as exactly 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. The mass of an atom in u is close to, but not exactly, its mass number, because binding energy contributes to the nuclear mass. The atomic mass on the periodic table is the weighted average over the natural abundances of the isotopes:

body.eq: average atomic mass = Σ (fractional abundance × isotope mass)

example.title: Average atomic mass of chlorine
example.problem: Chlorine is 75.77% ³⁵Cl (34.969 u) and 24.23% ³⁷Cl (36.966 u). Find the average atomic mass.
solution: No single chlorine atom has mass 35.45 u. Mass spectrometry shows two peaks, at 35 and 37, in a 3:1 ratio.

example.title: Counting particles
example.problem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in a ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ ion?
example.solution: Iron has Z = 26, so 26 protons. Neutrons: 56 − 26 = 30. The ion has lost three electrons: 26 − 3 = 23 electrons.

sections.title: The periodic table
body: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number so that elements with similar chemical properties fall in the same column. The columns are **groups**, numbered 1 to 18; the rows are **periods**, numbered 1 to 7. The explanation of why properties repeat is in the chapter on atomic structure. Here we need only the layout.

list: **Metals** (left and center) are lustrous, conduct heat and electricity, are malleable and ductile, and tend to lose electrons. **Nonmetals** (upper right) are poor conductors and tend to gain electrons. **Metalloids**, a diagonal band including B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te, have intermediate properties; silicon is a semiconductor.
**Main-group elements** are Groups 1, 2 and 13–18. **Transition metals** fill the d block (Groups 3–12). The **lanthanides** and **actinides** form the two rows below the table.
Several groups have family names: Group 1 the **alkali metals** (Li, Na, K…), Group 2 the **alkaline earth metals**, Group 17 the **halogens** (F, Cl, Br, I) and Group 18 the **noble gases**.

body: Hydrogen is placed above Group 1 but is a nonmetal with its own chemistry. At room temperature only two elements are liquids, bromine and mercury; eleven are gases (H, N, O, F, Cl and the noble gases).

sections.title: Molecules, ions and chemical formulas
body: A **molecule** is a group of atoms held together by covalent bonds that behaves as a unit. A **molecular formula** gives the number of each type of atom (glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆). A **structural formula** shows how they are connected. The **empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio (glucose: CH₂O). Seven elements exist as **diatomic molecules** under normal conditions: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. Some elements have several forms with different structures, called **allotropes**: O₂ and O₃ (ozone), or graphite, diamond and C₆₀.

An **ion** is an atom or group of atoms with a net charge. A **cation** has lost electrons and is positive; an **anion** has gained electrons and is negative. Atoms in main groups tend to form the ion that gives them the electron count of the nearest noble gas, so the charge can be predicted from the group.
Transition metals form cations of variable charge (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺). **Polyatomic ions** are covalently bonded groups carrying a charge. They must be memorized:

An **ionic compound** is a lattice of cations and anions with no discrete molecules, so its formula (a **formula unit**) gives only the ratio of ions. The ratio is set by charge neutrality: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ give Al₂O₃, because 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Polyatomic ions are enclosed in parentheses when more than one is needed: Ca₃(PO₄)₂.

sections.title: Naming compounds
body: Systematic names let a chemist reconstruct a formula from a name and the reverse.

Name the cation, then the anion. A monatomic cation takes the name of the element. If the metal can form more than one ion, the charge is given in Roman numerals (the **Stock system**): FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride, FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride. Monatomic anions take the stem of the element plus -ide: chloride, oxide, sulfide, nitride. Polyatomic ions keep their names. Fe₂(SO₄)₃ is iron(III) sulfate; NH₄NO₃ is ammonium nitrate.

Two nonmetals: name the first element, then the second with -ide, using Greek prefixes for the number of atoms (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-, hepta-, octa-, nona-, deca-). Mono- is dropped on the first element. CO is carbon monoxide, N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide, P₄O₁₀ is tetraphosphorus decaoxide.

Binary acids are named hydro-…-ic acid in water solution: HCl is hydrochloric acid. For an acid derived from an oxoanion, -ate becomes -ic and -ite becomes -ous: H₂SO₄ is sulfuric acid (from sulfate), H₂SO₃ is sulfurous acid (from sulfite), HNO₃ is nitric acid, HClO₄ is perchloric acid.
Some ionic solids incorporate water in the crystal. CuSO₄·5H₂O is copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate.

example.title: Names and formulas
example.problem: Name Mg(NO₃)₂ and N₂O₅. Write the formulas of copper(I) oxide and ammonium sulfide.
solution: Mg(NO₃)₂ is ionic, magnesium nitrate (Mg²⁺ takes no Roman numeral because it has only one common charge). N₂O₅ is dinitrogen pentoxide.
Copper(I) is Cu⁺ and oxide is O²⁻, so the formula is Cu₂O. Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and sulfide is S²⁻, so the formula is (NH₄)₂S.

check.why: SO₄²⁻ is sulfate. One Fe²⁺ balances one SO₄²⁻.

sections.title: The mole and molar mass
body: Atoms are far too small to count or weigh individually, so chemists count them in bulk. One **mole** is the amount of substance containing as many entities as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. That number is **Avogadro’s constant**:

The **molar mass** M of a substance is the mass of one mole, in g mol⁻¹. For an element it is numerically equal to the atomic mass in u. For a compound it is the sum over the formula: for CaCO₃, 40.08 + 12.01 + 3(16.00) = 100.09 g mol⁻¹. The mole is the bridge between the atomic scale and the laboratory scale.

quiz.q: Millikan's oil-drop experiment contributed which result to the discovery of the electron?
quiz.a: The charge of a single electron, which with Thomson's e/m gave the electron's mass
wrong: The charge-to-mass ratio of the electron
Proof that atoms contain a small, dense, positive nucleus
The mass of the proton relative to the electron
quiz.why: Thomson measured only the ratio e/m. Millikan found that droplet charges are whole multiples of 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and dividing that charge by e/m gives the mass.

quiz.q: Suppose the plum-pudding model were correct. In the gold-foil experiment the alpha particles would have
quiz.a: been deflected only slightly, since the positive charge would be spread thinly through each atom
wrong: bounced straight back from a fraction of the atoms
passed through undeflected, because gold atoms are neutral overall
been deflected only when they hit an embedded electron
quiz.why: A diffuse positive charge cannot exert a strong enough force to turn a fast alpha particle through a large angle. The observed back-scattering required the charge to be concentrated.

quiz.q: An atom is roughly 10⁵ times wider than its nucleus. If the nucleus were scaled up to a sphere 2 cm across, the atom would be about
How many protons, neutrons and electrons does a ⁵²Cr³⁺ ion have?
quiz.why: Chromium has Z = 24, so 24 protons and 52 − 24 = 28 neutrons. A 3+ charge means three electrons have been lost: 24 − 3 = 21.

quiz.q: Copper has isotopes ⁶³Cu (62.930 u, 69.15%) and ⁶⁵Cu (64.928 u, 30.85%). What is the average atomic mass?
quiz.why: 0.6915 × 62.930 + 0.3085 × 64.928 = 43.52 + 20.03 = 63.55 u. The plain mean of the two masses, 63.93 u, ignores the abundances.

quiz.q: An element has two isotopes with masses 50.0 u and 52.0 u, and its average atomic mass is 51.5 u. Which isotope is more abundant?
quiz.why: The average lies three-quarters of the way from 50.0 to 52.0, so the heavier isotope has a fractional abundance of 0.75. An equal mix would average 51.0 u.

quiz.q: The periodic table lists chlorine at 35.45 u. Which statement about this value is false?
quiz.a: Individual chlorine atoms have a mass of 35.45 u
wrong: It is a weighted average over naturally occurring isotopes
A mass spectrum of chlorine shows peaks near 35 u and 37 u
It lies closer to 35 u because ³⁵Cl is more abundant
quiz.why: No atom has mass 35.45 u. Each atom is ³⁵Cl or ³⁷Cl, and 35.45 u is the abundance-weighted average of the two.

quiz.q: Which of these elements is classified as a metalloid?
quiz.why: The metalloids form a diagonal band including B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te. Aluminum and gallium are metals, and phosphorus is a nonmetal.

quiz.q: Which element should be chemically most similar to calcium (Z = 20)?
quiz.why: Elements in the same group have similar chemistry, and strontium is in Group 2 below calcium. Neighbors in atomic number lie in different groups.

quiz.q: What is the correct formula of ammonium phosphate?
quiz.why: NH₄⁺ is 1+ and PO₄³⁻ is 3−, so three ammonium ions balance one phosphate. The polyatomic cation needs parentheses when more than one is used.

quiz.q: Which pair are allotropes of the same element?
quiz.why: Allotropes are different structural forms of one element. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes, which differ in neutron number, not in structure.

quiz.q: Which description of solid NaCl is correct?
quiz.a: A lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, with the formula giving only the 1:1 ratio
wrong: Separate NaCl molecules joined by covalent bonds
A lattice of neutral Na and Cl atoms
Pairs of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that each form a discrete molecule
quiz.why: An ionic compound has no discrete molecules. Its formula unit gives the ratio of ions that makes the lattice electrically neutral.

quiz.q: What is the name of Cu₂S?
quiz.why: S²⁻ needs +2 in total, which two Cu⁺ ions supply. A metal that can form several ions takes a Roman numeral, and prefixes are for molecular compounds.

quiz.q: HNO₂ is derived from the nitrite ion. What is its name?
quiz.why: For oxoacids, -ite becomes -ous and -ate becomes -ic. Nitric acid is HNO₃, from nitrate.

quiz.q: What is the molar mass of Ca₃(PO₄)₂? (Ca 40.08, P 30.97, O 16.00 g/mol)
quiz.why: 3(40.08) + 2(30.97) + 8(16.00) = 120.24 + 61.94 + 128.00 = 310.18. The subscript outside the parentheses multiplies both P and the four O in the phosphate.

quiz.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in 4.50 g of water (M = 18.02 g/mol)?
quiz.why: n(H₂O) = 4.50/18.02 = 0.250 mol, so n(H) = 0.500 mol and N = 0.500 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³. The value 1.50 × 10²³ counts molecules, not H atoms.

quiz.q: What is the mass of one CO₂ molecule (M = 44.01 g/mol)?
quiz.why: Mass per molecule is molar mass divided by N_A: 44.01 g/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 2.65 × 10²⁵.

quiz.q: How many grams of water are in 25.0 g of CuSO₄·5H₂O (M = 249.7 g/mol; H₂O = 18.02 g/mol)?
quiz.why: Water makes up 5(18.02)/249.7 = 36.1% of the hydrate's mass, so 25.0 × 0.361 = 9.02 g. The 16.0 g figure is the anhydrous CuSO₄ in the sample.

summary: Thomson found the electron, Rutherford found the nucleus and Chadwick found the neutron. Nearly all the mass is in a nucleus about 10⁵ times smaller than the atom.
Atomic number Z is the number of protons. Isotopes differ in neutron number. Average atomic mass weights each isotope by abundance.
The periodic table has groups (columns) and periods (rows). Metals are at left and center, nonmetals at upper right.
Main-group ions have predictable charges. Ionic compounds are electrically neutral and are named from the cation, then the anion. Molecular compounds use Greek prefixes.
One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ entities. n = m/M converts between mass and moles.

problems.q: Complete the table for ¹³¹I⁻, ⁵⁹Co²⁺ and ³¹P: number of protons, neutrons and electrons in each.
problems.solution: ¹³¹I⁻: Z = 53, N = 131 − 53 = 78, electrons 53 + 1 = 54. ⁵⁹Co²⁺: Z = 27, N = 32, electrons 25. ³¹P: Z = 15, N = 16, electrons 15.

problems.q: Gallium has two stable isotopes, ⁶⁹Ga (68.926 u) and ⁷¹Ga (70.925 u). The average atomic mass is 69.723 u. Find the percentage abundances.
Name (a) NaClO, (b) Cr₂O₃, (c) SF₆, (d) Ca(HCO₃)₂. Write formulas for (e) lithium nitride and (f) tin(IV) chloride.
